headline: Office Workers Now Submit Timesheets via Scheduled Ethernet Docks
deck: In the latest escalation of port disputes, routine tasks morph into bureaucratic battlegrounds.
article:
As the Ethernet conflict rages, workers must now book municipal dock slots to file timesheets. What once took ten minutes now demands a reservation form, three witnesses, and a notary stamp.

Wait times at the strip-mall kiosk average 47 minutes. Sally G. Porter, office manager at Loop & Wire Corp, said, "I set aside my morning just to fill forms that used to take one signature."

HOAs have begun holding quarterly hearings on backyard cable runs. Board member Gerald M. Socket explained, "Unregulated cords invite disorder, and the hearings give the committee something to do besides argue about lawn ornaments."

Cable providers are striking over access rights, leaving commuters worried their hours will go unrecorded if they cannot reach a port. The result is a city where every extension cord now requires paperwork and patience.
author: Clive T. Cable, Senior Bureaucratic Correspondent

oped.title: Ethernet Docks: Discipline's Last Redoubt
oped.author: Lord Reginald Portly, Emeritus Dockmaster of the Imperial Cabling Institute
oped.body: The latest port disputes reveal nothing so much as workers' ingratitude toward scheduled Ethernet docks. Far from bureaucratic excess, these timed slots instill the very tethering our cable-only civilization requires. Without them, employees would loiter at walls, inventing excuses instead of submitting timesheets. As the sole holder of the 7:45 a.m. premium port in my building, I find the system perfectly fair; complaints arise only from those whose flimsy cables and poorer planning cause backups. The obvious remedy is to auction remaining slots to the highest bidder each morning, guaranteeing access for serious professionals like myself while teaching the rest fiscal responsibility. Progress demands sacrifice, preferably by others.

classifieds.text: Help Wanted: Dock Scheduler needed at FinCorp to arbitrate Ethernet port bookings for weekly timesheets. Must resolve union fights over RJ-45 slots; overtime paid in extra cable length.
For Sale: 25-foot reinforced Ethernet leash with built-in timestamp printer. Barely used after last port dispute; owner switching to paper timesheets. $120, desperate to untether desk.
Lost & Found: Misplaced timesheet approval form from Ethernet Dock #4, last seen during 4-hour queue. Reward: one free docking slot if returned before Friday's schedule locks.
Personals: Cable-tethered analyst seeks after-hours docking partner. Bring your own extension cord; must share port access during peak timesheet windows. No wireless romantics.

panels.caption: Worker yanks cable: "Dock 3 slot's mine at noon. Timesheet or HR voids the week."
Manager overrides the port: "Executive reports bumped you. File next quarter—if the cable's free."
Worker, fused to the wall: "My resignation's queued behind the printer jam. See you in 2027."

stories.headline: Payroll Departments Add Ethernet Slot Lotteries for Timesheet Uploads
stories.deck: Firms report fewer late submissions but higher rates of employee no-shows at reserved ports.
stories.article:
Accounting firms now run weekly lotteries for dock reservations after staff missed their 15-minute windows. Priority numbers favor tenure and commute distance; winners receive printed slips at reception.

Processing delays dropped 22 percent, yet one Chicago office carries a waiting list into the next fiscal quarter for overtime approvals.

stories.headline: Thieves Target Park Benches With Jack Posts During Peak Commuter Hours
stories.deck: Stolen cable reels now account for 18 percent of reported property crimes near municipal transit hubs.
stories.article:
Police report rising thefts of unattended Ethernet reels at downtown benches. The new booking rules force users to linger, creating easy targets.

A Denver precinct now requires serial-number registration before any laptop connects at public posts.

stories.headline: Bookstores Install Wall-Mounted Docks for Self-Publishing Authors
stories.deck: Poetry readings now require advance sign-ups for both seating and cable time.
stories.article:
College-town bookstores added ports near writing tables so authors can upload manuscripts during scheduled 45-minute blocks. Staff interleave sessions between customer hours.

One Seattle shop now hands out extension cords with staff picks during evening events.
